title: SmartPlayer — Turning Model Outputs into User-Facing Analysis
context: At a sports performance platform, the core computer vision model produced rich biomechanical data, but end users (coaches, athletes) could not interpret the raw outputs. The product needed a layer that translated model results into actionable, understandable feedback.
ownership: Owned the product definition for the user-facing analysis interface, including information architecture, display logic, and interpretation thresholds.
actions: Defined what model outputs should surface to users and how, established display thresholds for what constitutes meaningful signal vs. noise, wrote the feature specs and acceptance criteria for the interpretation layer, collaborated with ML and engineering to map outputs to UX states, and ran structured QA cycles to validate output accuracy and usability.
result: Shipped a working interpretation layer that made complex model output readable and credible to non-technical end users. Reduced support-related confusion around output interpretation significantly.
metrics: Measurable reduction in interpretation-related support tickets. Improved session completion rates for coached workflows.
strengthNotes: Strong example of AI product work, output trust, and translating technical complexity for end users. Good for AI PM, platform PM, or technical PM roles.
risks: Avoid overstating model ownership — the candidate defined the product layer, not the model architecture itself.

title: Voice Assist — Feedback System Product Definition
context: The platform needed an in-session feedback delivery mechanism that could convert system outputs (scores, flags, measurements) into verbal coaching cues delivered to the user in real time.
ownership: Owned the product requirements and logic definition for the feedback system, including coverage, verbosity, specificity, tone calibration, and persona variation.
actions: Defined the feedback taxonomy and output logic. Built heuristic input mapping for when and how the system should trigger different feedback types. Designed persona configurations for different user contexts (e.g., beginner vs. competitive athlete). Iterated based on usability testing and operational feedback from field deployments.
result: Delivered a structured feedback system that could produce contextually appropriate, well-calibrated output across varied user contexts. Enabled the platform to move from generic feedback to targeted coaching language.
metrics: Increased feedback relevance ratings in user testing. Reduced 'confusing feedback' flags from field operators.
strengthNotes: Direct evidence of feedback system product work, AI output calibration, and user-centered design for technically complex outputs.
risks: Do not use RVSE or legacy terminology. Frame in terms of coverage, verbosity, specificity, result, encouragement, tone, cadence, personas, heuristic input mapping.

title: QA and Diagnostic Workflows for Model Behavior
context: As the platform scaled, model output reliability became a critical trust issue. Inconsistent outputs, edge-case failures, and data quality problems were eroding confidence internally and with customers.
ownership: Led the definition of QA workflows and diagnostic processes for evaluating model output quality. Owned acceptance criteria and testing logic for output validation.
actions: Designed systematic QA processes for validating model outputs against known ground truths. Created structured test case libraries and edge case documentation. Built internal tooling requirements for output diagnostics. Established criteria for when outputs should be flagged, suppressed, or surfaced with caveats. Trained team on evaluation standards.
result: Significantly improved internal confidence in model output quality. Reduced release-blocking QA failures. Created repeatable evaluation processes that could scale with the team.
metrics: Reduction in post-release output quality incidents. Improved time-to-diagnosis for model behavior issues.
strengthNotes: Excellent story for roles requiring rigor around AI systems, data quality, and trust. Works for AI PM, Platform PM, TPM roles.
risks: Make clear this is product QA leadership, not engineering QA. Candidate owned the process and criteria, not the test automation code.

title: Onsite Workflow Design — Capture and Calibration Systems
context: The platform required physical camera setup and calibration at customer sites before data collection could begin. Early onsite workflows were inconsistent, error-prone, and resulted in poor data quality that downstream model performance depended on.
ownership: Owned the operational workflow design and product requirements for the onsite capture and calibration process.
actions: Mapped the full onsite operator workflow from arrival through calibration completion. Identified key failure points in existing setup flows. Defined structured operator checklists and validation steps. Specified the software-side calibration UX including status indicators, error states, and retry logic. Worked with engineering to build validation feedback into the capture flow.
result: Reduced calibration failures and setup errors significantly. Improved data quality entering the model pipeline. Made the onsite process trainable and repeatable for new operators.
metrics: Reduction in onsite setup errors. Improved data validity rates from capture sessions.
strengthNotes: Strong for operationally complex product roles. Shows PM ability to own end-to-end workflow design in field environments.
risks: Frame as operational product work, not hardware or physical setup. Focus on workflow design and the software/UX layer.

title: PRD and Roadmap Structure — From Ambiguity to Documented Product Direction
context: Early in the platform's development, product direction was largely in engineers' heads with minimal structured documentation. As the team scaled and external stakeholders needed visibility, the lack of formal product documentation became a risk.
ownership: Owned the transition to structured product documentation including PRDs, roadmap artifacts, user stories, and acceptance criteria. Defined documentation standards for the team.
actions: Introduced PRD templates calibrated to the team's existing workflow. Backfilled documentation for in-flight features. Defined user story and acceptance criteria formats. Created a roadmap structure that made prioritization visible and defensible. Facilitated prioritization sessions with technical and business stakeholders.
result: Improved cross-functional alignment on what was being built and why. Reduced engineering rework caused by unclear requirements. Gave stakeholders a credible visibility layer into the product.
metrics: Reduction in requirement-related rework cycles. Faster onboarding time for new engineering and product team members.
strengthNotes: Shows structured PM execution and ability to bring clarity to ambiguous environments. Relevant for any PM role, especially in scaling or early-stage contexts.
risks: Keep the focus on impact — not just process for its own sake. Connect documentation to better decisions and outcomes.

title: Stakeholder Alignment on Model Interpretation Standards
context: Disagreements between ML, product, and business stakeholders about what the model output 'meant' and how to present it to users created recurring conflict and slowed product decisions.
ownership: Facilitated alignment across ML, product, engineering, and commercial stakeholders on shared interpretation standards and display criteria.
actions: Identified the root cause as different mental models of what model outputs represented. Organized structured sessions to align on definitions and thresholds. Translated ML team's probabilistic framing into product-compatible language. Produced a shared reference document that all teams could use as a decision anchor. Used this shared standard to resolve downstream product disputes faster.
result: Reached durable alignment on output interpretation standards. Reduced recurring disputes about display thresholds and user-facing language. Enabled faster product decisions by establishing shared ground truth.
metrics: Reduction in cross-team disagreement cycles on display criteria. Faster time-to-decision on output-related product questions.
strengthNotes: Strong for stakeholder management and cross-functional alignment questions. Shows ability to resolve technical ambiguity with business consequences.
risks: Keep focus on the PM-owned facilitation and documentation, not the technical resolution itself.

title: Prioritization Under Constraint — Scoping a Limited Engineering Cycle
context: During a product planning cycle with a constrained engineering team, there were more feature requests, bug fixes, and infrastructure needs than capacity. Stakeholders across commercial, ML, and operations had competing priorities.
ownership: Led the prioritization process, defined the framework for evaluation, and owned the final recommendation to leadership.
actions: Audited all competing requests and mapped them against user impact, technical risk, and commercial dependency. Applied a scoring framework weighted by customer-facing value and delivery risk. Ran structured prioritization reviews with each stakeholder group. Made and defended the final call with clear rationale. Communicated tradeoffs explicitly to all stakeholders.
result: Delivered a prioritized plan that all major stakeholders understood and could work within, even when they disagreed with specific decisions. The cycle shipped on scope without post-hoc scrambling.
metrics: Shipped planned scope within the cycle. No major re-prioritization mid-cycle. Stakeholder satisfaction maintained despite cuts.
strengthNotes: Clean prioritization story with clear decision ownership. Works well for product sense and execution questions.
risks: Be specific about the criteria used — avoid sounding like a framework recitation. Ground it in what the actual tradeoffs were.

title: Failure — Misreading User Needs in Early Feature Design
context: An early version of a user-facing analysis feature was designed based on internal assumptions about what users wanted to see, without sufficient validation from actual users. The feature shipped but adoption was low and user feedback was negative.
ownership: Owned the product definition for the feature, including the assumption that users would find the raw metric display useful.
actions: Recognized the adoption and feedback signals quickly. Ran retrospective discovery sessions with users to understand the actual gap. Identified that users needed interpretive guidance, not raw numbers. Rebuilt the product requirements around the interpreted output model and drove a redesign.
result: Redesigned feature showed significantly improved adoption and user satisfaction. Established a principle for the team that raw model output is never a finished product feature.
metrics: Feature adoption increase post-redesign. Reduction in negative user feedback on the specific module.
strengthNotes: Honest failure story with clear learning and recovery. Shows self-awareness and ability to course-correct. Good for behavioral questions about failure or mistakes.
risks: Own the mistake clearly — don't deflect to users or process. Make the learning and response the strong part.
